No tickets when we boarded / I had only Rs 100 in my pocket and / a train to Aurangabad.

questions.solution_en:

Hence, option (b) is the correct answer.

The correct sentence is: I had only Rs 100 in my pocket and no tickets when we boarded a train to Aurangabad.

The woman to who I sold my house was a criminal.
questions.solution_en:
The sentence is: "The woman to who I sold my house was a criminal." The underlined segment "to who" is incorrect. In English, "who" is used as a subject, while "whom" is used as an object, especially after prepositions like "to." Here, "to" is a preposition, and the relative pronoun refers to "the woman," the object of the clause "I sold my house." Thus, "whom" is correct. The correct structure is "to whom I sold," making the sentence: "The woman to whom I sold my house was a criminal." Among the options:

to whom sold lacks the subject "I," making it grammatically incorrect.

No substitution is incorrect as "to who" is wrong.

to whom I sold is the correct structure.

questions.q_en:
In the following question, a sentence has been given in Direct/Indirect speech. Out of the four alternatives suggested, select the one which best expresses the same sentence in Indirect/Direct speech.

Dhoni said to Virat Kohli, “Will you do some work for me?”
options_en: Dhoni asked Virat Kohli whether he would like doing some work for him.
Dhoni asked Virat Kohli that if he will be doing some work for me.
Dhoni asked to Virat Kohli whether he will do some work for him.
Dhoni asked Virat Kohli whether he would do some work for him.
questions.solution_en:
In the case of Interrogative sentences like this, said in Direct Speech is changed into enquired (of), wanted to know, asked, etc.

In Indirect speech, the verb is always placed after the subject, unlike in Direct Speech.

If there is a question in the Direct Speech whose answer can come as Yes or No in the Indirect Speech, we should use the conjunctions if or whether.

For example:

Ravi said to me, Is she studying? (Direct Speech)

Ravi asked me if she was studying. (Indirect Speech)

Also, the sentence in the Direct Speech is in the tense. So, the tense in the Indirect Speech should be in the tense.

The following things in the sentence should change when changed from Direct speech to Indirect Speech:

‘you’ changes into ‘he’ ‘said to’ into ‘asked’."

Therefore, the correct answer is option (d).

Choose the option that is the correct passive form of the given sentence.

The walls feature topographical maps of various regions of India.
options_en: Topographical maps of various regions of India were featured on the walls.
Topographical maps of various regions of India are featuring on the walls.
Topographical maps of various regions of India are being featured on the walls.
Topographical maps of various regions of India are featured on the walls.
questions.solution_en:
The sentence is in the simple present tense (present tense form 'maps'). Let's see the sentence structure for change of voice:

Active voice construct: Subject + present tense form of verb + Object -> 'The walls' is the Subject; 'topographical maps of various regions of India' is the Object.

Passive voice construct: Object + is/am/are + past participle of verb + by + Subject

The correct passive form is - [Topographical maps of various regions of India are featured on the walls.]

The answer is option (d).

A. On the afternoon of that eventful day, I stood on the porch, dumb, expectant and guessed vaguely from my mother's signs and from the hurrying to and fro in the house that something unusual was about to happen, so I went to the door and waited on the steps.

B. I did not know what the future held of marvel or surprise for me and anger and bitterness had preyed upon me continually for weeks and a deep languor had succeeded this passionate struggle.

C. The most important day I remember in all my life is the one on which my teacher, Anne Mansfield Sullivan, came to me and I am filled with wonder when I consider the immeasurable contrasts between the two lives which it connects and it was the third of March, 1887, three months before I was seven years old.

D. The afternoon sun penetrated the mass of honeysuckle that covered the porch, and fell on my upturned face and my fingers lingered almost unconsciously on the familiar leaves and blossoms which had just come forth to greet the sweet southern spring.
questions.solution_en:
'C' is the first sentence as it begins the topic of discussion i.e. the important day for a person, 'A' describes the afternoon of the important day so it will be the second sentence of the paragraph. 'D' describes more about the afternoon that was described in 'A'. 'B' is an independent sentence so it can be kept at the end of the paragraph. Therefore, the correct order is CADB.

Hence, option (c) is correct.

questions.q_en:
Directions [Set of 4 Questions]: Read the given passage and answer the questions that follow.

With cracked plaster and peeling paint, I considered what I could say. Water damage would've been the easy answer, but I opted for the truth: "My phone rang." As expected, these words settled somewhere beyond her reach, so she gave my comment its only sensible response: "Maybe you should turn down the ringer." "Come here, let me explain why I hate phones, and why my father is to blame. He was a troubled man," I said, because that's how it had been said to me. She listened with attentive eyes, but I knew she'd be confused by what I said next: "And he'd play Nulla in Mundo Pax Sincera. Over and over." She lowered her head in search of a link and looked up when she found one. "Is that solitaire?" This time I allowed a smile. "Sometimes he'd conduct an invisible orchestra, waving arms in an erratic fashion, and sometimes he'd sit and listen. But Nulla in Mundo Pax Sincera, that one commanded a different reaction. From the start, he stood at full attention, motionless until the end. It went like this for a long time, then he left."

"I soon became his replacement. I'd sit in the study and listen to his music. One evening mother said he wanted to talk to me. I asked if I was going to see him and she said that he'd call. I asked if I could use the phone in his study and she said I could." At this point my companion, attentive as ever, offered her second assumption of the evening, and though more likely than the first, it was just as wrong: "And he never called and that's why you hate phones." No, that's not why. "When mother told me he was on the line, I rushed to the study and dropped the needle on Nulla in Mundo Pax Sincera, then picked up the phone. He didn't say hello or ask how I was, he only said that there's no peace in the world. He'd looked, it wasn't there, not for him." With her final assumption, she came closer to the truth: "So phones remind you of your father, and that's why you hate them."

"That's part of it," I said, "but there's more. He said he could hear Vivaldi in the background and told me to keep listening, that aria was on to something. Then he said goodbye to me and mother and everyone else. Forever. He found his peace." The music prevented a silence that would've felt more comfortable, then it finally stopped and I let the silence prevail. And there we sat, speaking without speaking, until the silence was shattered by a ring. I stood and walked to the phone, picked it up, not just the receiver, but all of it, and paused to admire the artistry.

According to the passage, what is Nulla in Mundo Pax Sincera?
questions.solution_en:
The passage conveys the father's passion for music. The first paragraph states that "Sometimes he'd conduct an invisible orchestra, waving arms in an erratic fashion, and sometimes he'd sit and listen. But Nulla in Mundo Pax Sincera, that one commanded a different reaction." From this part, we can conclude that Nulla in Mundo Pax Sincera is a kind of music.

Hence, option (b) is the correct answer.

questions.q_en:
Change the following sentence into superlative degree.

No other mountain in the world is as high as the Mount Everest.
options_en: No other mountain is highest than Mount Everest.
Mount Everest is the highest mountain in the world.
Mount Everest is higher than any other mountain in the world.
Mount Everest is high mountain in the world.
questions.solution_en:
The original sentence is in comparative degree ("as high as"). The superlative degree compares one item to all others, using "the + -est" or "most."

A. No other mountain is highest than: Incorrect, as "highest" (superlative) doesn't pair with "than."

B. Mount Everest is the highest mountain in the world: Correctly uses "the highest" to indicate Mount Everest surpasses all others.

C. Mount Everest is higher than any other mountain: Comparative, not superlative.

D. Mount Everest is high mountain: Lacks the superlative and an article ("a").

The correct superlative form is option B.

So, the correct sentence is: Since implementing the new automated quality control system, the factory has reported significantly fewer complaints from customers regarding product defects, which is a wonderful improvement.

Hence, the most appropriate choice is a) fewer complaints from customers.

The placement of "ever" at the end is incorrect, making this segment erroneous.

· Option 2: "her friend, 'You're" - This segment is grammatically correct. It's part of the sentence structure where "she said to her friend" introduces the dialogue, and "You're" is the contraction of "You are," which is appropriate in the quoted speech.

· Option 4: "the sweetest person" - This segment is correct as well. It's part of the quoted speech and is grammatically sound.

Thus, the error lies in Option 1 due to the incorrect placement of "ever."

b) Dissatisfied - means not pleased or happy with a situation or outcome. This is the opposite of "complacent."

a) Smug - having or showing an excessive pride in oneself or one's achievements.

c) Satisfied - contented; pleased.

d) Complete - means having all the necessary or appropriate parts. This is an unrelated word.

The complete sentence is: The manager was deeply dissatisfied with the team's very poor quarterly performance report.

Hence, option (b) is the correct answer.

questions.q_en:
Select the option that expresses the given sentence in present tense form.

We received a lot of expressions of support for our campaign.
options_en: We will be receiving a lot of expressions of support for our campaign.
We have received a lot of expressions of support for our campaign.
We had received a lot of expressions of support for our campaign.
We were receiving a lot of expressions of support for our campaign.
questions.solution_en:
The correct option that expresses the given sentence in present tense form is (b). Option (b) changes the verb "received" (past tense) to "have received" (present perfect tense). The present perfect tense is used to talk about actions that were completed at some unspecified time before the present moment and have relevance to the present. It is formed using the auxiliary verb "have" (or "has" for singular subjects) followed by the past participle of the main verb (in this case, "received"). Option (a) is in the future continuous tense ("will be" + present participle of the verb). Option (c) is in the past perfect tense ("had" + past participle of the verb). Option (d) is in the past continuous tense ("were"/ "was" + present participle of the verb). Hence, (b) is the correct answer.

NOTE:

Auxiliary verb: A verb that gives grammatical information that is not given by the main verb of a sentence. It supports the main verb. Auxiliary verbs help to form the various tenses, moods, and voices of other verbs. The principal ones are be, do, and have. Example: She will sing a song tomorrow. Here, 'will' is the auxiliary verb that supports the main verb 'sing'.

Participle: A word formed from a verb (e.g. going, gone, being, been) and used as an adjective (e.g. working woman, burnt toast) or a noun (e.g. good breeding). In English, participles are also used to make compound verb forms (e.g. is going, has been). Consider the sentences given below:

Dancing at the party, the women fell on the ground.

Encouraged by her parents, Rita went on to pursue her passion.

The highlighted word in the first sentence is of the form Verb + ing and is used as a present participle. It is used to denote an action that is going on or incomplete or imperfect.

The highlighted word in the second sentence is of the form verb + ed. It is used as a past participle. It denotes the completed action or state of the thing spoken of.

A past participle ends with the following: -ed, -d, -t, -en, or -n.

One should take great care and never get confused between a gerund and a present participle. They use the same forms but perform different functions: a gerund is a verbal noun, while a present participle is a verbal adjective.
